prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, opening a new regime of precision time and frequency measurement

statement.case_for: I ranked IceCube first and the lattice clock third in my opening ballot, but after reading all eight ballots I move the lattice clock to the head of my configuration. It is the only shortlisted candidate that all seven ranking members place in the top five and that five place in the top three, so it is the one most likely to hold a committee together. On the merits it is a new measurement technique in the sense I respect most: Katori's magic-wavelength trap removes the light shift that otherwise limits a lattice, and Ye's group turned that into clocks at about 1e-18 fractional uncertainty with many atoms interrogated at once. The result has been reproduced and surpassed by several independent laboratories, which is the standard I apply to any claimed advance. It has already produced centimetre-scale tests of gravitational time dilation and constraints on drifting constants, and the redefinition of the second is being prepared. Attribution is also unusually clean: two people, one proposing the scheme and one driving it to record performance, with the comb prize of 2005 covering a separate invention.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the committee has already recognised optical frequency combs (2005) and the control of single trapped ions (2012), so a critic can call lattice clocks an incremental step in a field that has been honoured twice. It is also a precision-measurement invention rather than the discovery of a new phenomenon, and the formal redefinition of the SI second has not yet happened. Finally, atomic clocks are outside my own expertise, so I am leaning on Lindroth, Kroll and Johansson for the priority history, including the claims of Lemonde, Ludlow and the ion-clock groups that the credited names leave out.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the lattice clock first as a genuine conceptual step, combining the magic wavelength with Lamb-Dicke confinement of many atoms, and ranks IceCube sixth because source identification is thin and recognition may be somewhat early.
responses.response: I accept her physics argument on the clock and it is what moved me. On IceCube I partly disagree: the prize would be for the discovery of the diffuse astrophysical flux and the technique, which is secure at far above five sigma, not for a complete source catalogue. Her point about the overlap with 2005 and 2012 is the real test, and I think the answer is that the lattice scheme is a distinct invention. I would still like her to say whether she would defend that distinction against a colleague who sees it as one field honoured three times.

responses.point: Danielsson puts IceCube first as a measurement driven by nature that opened a new window, and he flags the attribution among Halzen, Karle, Spiering and the AMANDA and DUMAND pioneers as delicate.
responses.response: I agree on the window and I voted the same way. My qualification is about timing and attribution, not worth: independent confirmation by KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD is still thin, and the three-person cut among IceCube leaders and earlier pioneers is more arbitrary than the Katori and Ye pairing. I would keep IceCube as my first alternative and revisit it if the committee wants an astrophysics prize this year, but I do not want to push it ahead of a candidate with broader support and a cleaner credit.

responses.point: Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron optics first as a tool that opens a door, and she would credit Rose, Haider and Urban while questioning an IceCube credit that includes Spiering.
responses.response: I respect the instrument argument, and I ranked it fifth myself. I do not think it should lead, because the STEM corrector side (Krivanek) is missing from the credited names, and chemistry's 2017 cryo-EM prize and the 1986 Ruska precedent make the home and novelty arguable. On IceCube, I would resist dropping Spiering: his work on the Baikal and AMANDA telescopes was the groundwork the cubic-kilometre detector built on, so a two-name version would weaken the attribution rather than clean it.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as the natural continuation of the 2025 prize and discloses his own proximity to that community.
responses.response: I value the disclosure, and it is exactly why I would not count his first place as settled committee preference. My serious disagreement is on timing: a prize on superconducting circuits was awarded in 2025, and Kroll and Eriksson both worry about proximity, while only four members rank circuit QED at all. I cannot judge the Yale, ETH and Sherbrooke credit myself, so I defer to him on the facts but not on the conclusion that it is ready now.

uncertainties: Whether colleagues who know the field regard lattice clocks as distinct enough from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Priority history among Katori, Ye and the other early lattice-clock groups, which I cannot check from the supplied credit.
Whether the committee prefers to wait for the formal redefinition of the second.
If the committee wants a second part, whether Halzen, Karle and Spiering can fit alongside two clock laureates under the three-person limit; I do not see a clean way to do it.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the lattice clock. I work in the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations, not in IceCube, but astroparticle physics at KTH is close to the IceCube field, so colleagues should weigh my first-place ranking of B021 accordingly; no recusal seems required.
